lessons.title: Early Models of the Solar System
lessons.description: Ancient uses of Solar System cycles, the geocentric model, Ptolemy's epicycles and astronomical distance units.
lessons.content_html:
Ancient Astronomy — More Than Stargazing

Long before telescopes or scientific theory, civilisations around the world used the regular motions of the Sun, Moon and stars for entirely practical purposes. The patterns of the sky governed when to plant and harvest crops, when floods could be expected, and when religious festivals should be held. Astronomy was not a separate discipline — it was embedded in agriculture, religion and governance.

Ancient agricultural societies tracked the lunar calendar alongside the solar year. The lunar month (one cycle of phases, approximately 29.5 days) does not divide evenly into the solar year (approximately 365.25 days), so early astronomers devised intercalation — adding extra months periodically to keep the calendar aligned with the seasons. The Babylonian calendar used a 19-year cycle (the Metonic cycle, later named after the Greek astronomer Meton) in which 7 extra months were inserted, keeping the calendar accurate over the long term.

Stonehenge in Wiltshire is aligned so that the rising Sun at the summer solstice falls along the axis of the monument. Many ancient stone circles and temples show similar solar or lunar alignments — they served as fixed astronomical instruments for marking the solstices and equinoxes. The Egyptians aligned the Great Pyramid of Giza to the cardinal points of the compass with remarkable accuracy. The precision of these alignments demonstrates that ancient peoples had systematic knowledge of the apparent motions of the Sun and stars over decades.

A key practical challenge was that alignment points shift over centuries due to precession — the slow wobble of Earth’s rotation axis over a 26,000-year cycle. The north celestial pole migrates around the sky: today Polaris marks it, but in 3000 BCE the north pole was near the star Thuban in Draco. Ancient monuments calibrated to a particular stellar alignment become misaligned over long periods, which is why alignments of ancient sites must be interpreted with knowledge of the sky at the time of construction, not the present-day sky.

The Geocentric Model

Ancient Greek astronomers developed a formal mathematical model of the cosmos. The dominant view was the geocentric model — Earth stationary at the centre, with the Moon, Sun, planets and stars all orbiting it on great spheres. This model matched the obvious observation that Earth does not feel like it is moving, and the stars appear fixed rather than parallax-shifted (which the Greeks correctly noted would be expected if Earth moved around the Sun — but the parallax is too small to detect with the naked eye).

The Roman-Greek astronomer Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE) systematised the geocentric model in his great work the Almagest. To explain the observed retrograde motion of planets — which was puzzling if planets simply orbited Earth in perfect circles — Ptolemy introduced epicycles. A planet did not orbit Earth directly; instead it moved on a small circle (the epicycle) whose centre moved on a large circle (the deferent) around Earth. By choosing appropriate epicycle sizes and speeds, Ptolemy could predict planetary positions with reasonable accuracy for practical purposes such as astrology and calendar-making.

Key Fact

In Ptolemy’s geocentric model, planets move on small circles called epicycles whose centres travel on large circles (deferents) around Earth. This allowed the model to match the observed retrograde motion of planets without admitting that Earth orbited the Sun.

Scale of the Solar System — Astronomical Distance Units

Astronomy deals with distances far beyond everyday experience. Three units are used depending on the scale of interest:

The astronomical unit (AU) is defined as the mean distance from Earth to the Sun: approximately \(1.5 \times 10^8\) km. The AU is the most natural unit for planetary distances — Jupiter is about 5.2 AU from the Sun, Neptune about 30 AU.

A light-year (l.y.) is the distance light travels in one year in a vacuum: approximately \(9.5 \times 10^{12}\) km. The nearest star system beyond the Sun, Alpha Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away. Light-years are practical for describing distances to individual stars and within our galaxy.

A parsec (pc) is the distance at which a star would appear to shift by one arcsecond of parallax as Earth moves 1 AU (one parsec = 3.26 light-years = approximately \(3.086 \times 10^{13}\) km). The parsec is the professional astronomer’s unit — it arises naturally from the parallax measurement method. Kiloparsecs (kpc) and megaparsecs (Mpc) are used for galactic and cosmological distances.

Comparing the units in context:

  • Earth to Sun: 1 AU = \(1.5 \times 10^8\) km
  • Earth to nearest star: 1.3 pc = 4.2 l.y. = \(4.0 \times 10^{13}\) km
  • Diameter of Milky Way: about 30 kpc (100,000 l.y.)
  • Distance to Andromeda Galaxy: about 778 kpc (2.5 million l.y.)
Key Fact

1 AU ≈ \(1.5 \times 10^8\) km  •  1 light-year ≈ \(9.5 \times 10^{12}\) km  •  1 parsec = 3.26 light-years. These three values will appear in calculation questions — learn them precisely.

Why the Geocentric Model Survived So Long

The geocentric model was not simply wrong and ignored — it was mathematically sophisticated and practically useful. With enough epicycles, Ptolemy’s model could be adjusted to match observations accurately. The model held philosophical authority from Aristotle (who argued that Earth must be at the centre as the heaviest element, and the heavens must move in perfect circles). It also had observational support of a kind: if Earth moved around the Sun, you would expect the nearby stars to shift against distant ones (stellar parallax) — but the parallax of even the nearest stars is tiny (less than one arcsecond) and was not detected until 1838, when the telescopes and measurement techniques were finally precise enough. The geocentric model therefore survived for about 1,400 years after Ptolemy, until Copernicus and later Kepler provided the heliocentric alternative in the 16th and 17th centuries.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Distance unit questions commonly appear as calculations. Make sure you know the three units and their values in km in standard form: AU = \(1.5 \times 10^8\) km; light-year = \(9.5 \times 10^{12}\) km; parsec = 3.26 l.y. Candidates often lose marks by writing \(1.5 \times 10^7\) (one power of ten short for AU) or \(9.5 \times 10^{11}\) for the light-year. When explaining why the geocentric model was accepted for so long, the key points are: it matched observations using epicycles, it had the authority of Aristotle, and stellar parallax is too small to detect with the naked eye.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ancient civilisations used the regular motions of the Sun, Moon and stars for agriculture, religion and timekeeping; ancient monuments such as Stonehenge show deliberate solar and lunar alignments.
  • Ptolemy’s geocentric model placed Earth at the centre, with planets on epicycles (small circles) whose centres orbit on deferents (large circles) around Earth, explaining retrograde motion without a heliocentric framework.
  • Astronomical distances are described in three units: 1 AU (≈ \(1.5 \times 10^8\) km), 1 light-year (≈ \(9.5 \times 10^{12}\) km), and 1 parsec (3.26 l.y.); the parsec is defined by stellar parallax geometry.

lessons.title: Planetary Motion and Gravity
lessons.description: Brahe, Copernicus, Kepler and Newton — how the heliocentric model was built, with Kepler's three laws worked through.
lessons.content_html:
The Scientific Revolution in Astronomy

The shift from the geocentric to the heliocentric model was not a single event — it was a 150-year process involving several scientists whose contributions built on each other in a remarkable chain. Understanding who did what, and why each step mattered, is central to this lesson.

Copernicus (1473–1543) published his heliocentric model in De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1543, the year of his death). He placed the Sun at the centre, with Earth and the other planets orbiting it. Crucially, he explained retrograde motion as a line-of-sight effect when Earth overtakes an outer planet — a far simpler explanation than Ptolemy’s epicycles. However, Copernicus still assumed perfectly circular orbits, which meant his predictions were not significantly more accurate than Ptolemy’s.

Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was the greatest naked-eye observer of his era. Working from the island of Hven in Denmark with instruments of his own design, he compiled two decades of planetary position data accurate to about one arcminute — roughly ten times more precise than any previous systematic record. Brahe himself favoured a hybrid model (planets orbit the Sun, but the Sun orbits a stationary Earth), but his data were the raw material that Kepler would use to demolish all circular-orbit models.

Key Fact

Tycho Brahe’s data were essential because only observations accurate to one arcminute or better could distinguish between circular and elliptical orbits. Without Brahe’s numbers, Kepler could not have shown that orbits are ellipses.

Kepler’s Three Laws

Kepler (1571–1630) worked as Brahe’s assistant, inheriting his data after Brahe’s death in 1601. After years of calculation, Kepler published his laws in 1609 and 1619. Each law replaced a previous assumption about planetary motion:

First Law: Each planet moves in an elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus of the ellipse. The Sun is not at the centre of the ellipse, but at one of its two foci. The point in the orbit nearest the Sun is called perihelion; the furthest point is called aphelion. For orbits around Earth (e.g. the Moon or artificial satellites), the equivalent terms are perigee and apogee. Earth's orbit is only slightly elliptical (eccentricity 0.017), but for some comets the eccentricity approaches 1, giving a very elongated orbit.

Second Law: A line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals. This means planets move faster when they are near perihelion (close to the Sun) and slower when they are near aphelion (far from the Sun). Earth moves at about 30.3 km s⁻1 in January (near perihelion) and 29.3 km s⁻1 in July (near aphelion). This explains why Northern Hemisphere winters (when Earth is near perihelion) are slightly shorter than summers — Earth covers the perihelion arc faster.

Kepler’s Third Law — Period and Distance

Third Law: The square of a planet’s orbital period is proportional to the cube of its mean orbital radius. In equation form:

$$\frac{T^2}{r^3} = \text{constant}$$

where T is the orbital period in years and r is the mean orbital radius in astronomical units. The constant is the same for all objects orbiting the same central body (the Sun). This is the most practically useful of the three laws because it allows you to calculate the orbital radius of any planet or moon if you can measure its orbital period, and vice versa.

Worked example: Mars has an orbital period of 1.881 years. Find its mean distance from the Sun in AU.

$$\frac{T^2}{r^3} = 1 \text{ (in the appropriate units)}$$ $$r^3 = T^2 = 1.881^2 = 3.538$$ $$r = \sqrt[3]{3.538} = 1.52 \text{ AU}$$

This matches the accepted value of 1.52 AU for Mars. Always state the formula, substitute, rearrange and give the final answer with units when answering calculation questions.

Key Fact

Kepler’s Third Law: \(T^2 / r^3 = \text{constant}\). For objects orbiting the Sun with T in years and r in AU, the constant = 1. So \(T^2 = r^3\). Rearrange to find T or r as required.

Newton’s Explanation — Universal Gravitation

Kepler’s laws were empirical — they described the data precisely but gave no reason why planets should obey these rules. Isaac Newton (1643–1727) provided the physical explanation with his law of universal gravitation, published in the Principia Mathematica (1687). Newton showed that any two masses attract each other with a gravitational force that:

  • increases with the mass of each object
  • decreases with the square of the distance between their centres (the inverse square law)

Newton demonstrated mathematically that if the gravitational force follows the inverse square law, then orbiting bodies must follow elliptical paths (Kepler’s first law) and the equal-areas law (second law) follows automatically from conservation of angular momentum. He also derived the constant in Kepler’s third law in terms of the mass of the central body and the gravitational constant G.

For a stable circular orbit, the gravitational force provides exactly the centripetal force needed to keep the orbiting body on its circular path. If the orbital speed is too low, gravity pulls the object inward (it spirals in or falls); if the speed is too high, the object escapes gravity and follows a parabolic or hyperbolic path. At exactly the right speed for the orbital radius, a stable circular orbit results. This is the principle behind the orbits of planets, moons, and artificial satellites.

The geocentric-to-heliocentric transition illustrates how science progresses: Copernicus proposed a new framework that was simpler in concept but initially not more accurate. Brahe’s meticulous observations provided the data needed to test models. Kepler found laws that fitted the data only when he abandoned the assumption of circular orbits — a result that required him to discard years of earlier work. Newton then explained why those laws hold, elevating them from description to physical theory. This chain — hypothesis, observation, law, theory — is a textbook example of the scientific method operating over multiple generations.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Kepler’s Third Law calculations are a reliable mark source if you learn the method: (1) state \(T^2 = r^3\) (in years and AU for Solar System problems); (2) substitute; (3) rearrange if asked for r (cube-root) or T (square-root); (4) give the answer with units. Common errors: forgetting to take the cube root when finding r, or the square root when finding T; using the wrong units (mixing km with AU). For extended-response questions asking you to ‘evaluate the contribution’ of Brahe, Kepler or Newton, link each to the data or laws that the next figure relied on: Brahe’s data → Kepler’s laws → Newton’s theory.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Copernicus proposed a Sun-centred Solar System; Tycho Brahe provided the most accurate naked-eye planetary data ever compiled; Kepler derived three empirical laws from that data; Newton explained those laws through universal gravitation and the inverse square law.
  • Kepler’s First Law: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus. Second Law: equal areas swept in equal times (planets move faster at perihelion). Third Law: \(T^2 / r^3 = \text{constant}\) (in AU and years, constant = 1 for Solar System objects).
  • Newton’s inverse square law of gravity explains why Kepler’s laws hold: gravity provides the centripetal force for stable orbits, and its inverse square dependence on distance mathematically produces elliptical orbits and the equal-areas rule.
